questions.stem:
The following passage is from a play called The Age of Leisure. The numbers in square brackets show the line numbers.

PASSAGE

The scene is an office. JANE is seated at a desk. She is examining papers and card
indexes. She is a pretty, efficient girl and is keen on her job. There is a knock at
the door.
JANE [in a pleasant voice]. Come in.
[Muggs enters. He is a middle-aged man. JANE looks him up and down.]  [5]
JANE. What can I do for you?
MUGGS [nervously]. You know, miss.
JANE. Now, now Muggs, really.
MUGGS [wheedling]. Jist a job o’work, miss, for the luv —
JANE. Muggs, you must face the facts. In the working-age you were a plumber,  [10]
weren’t you?
MUGGS. Yes, miss, a poor, well-meanin’, ’armless plumber.
JANE. Well, as you know perfectly well, plumbing has been abolished. And if
plumbing is unnecessary, so are plumbers.
MUGGS. I don’t want to contradict ye, miss, but there was a bit o’ a frost last night.  [15]
Couldn’t you let a pipe or two burst?
JANE. There are no pipes to burst, Muggs. We live in the pipeless age, my good man.
MUGGS [hopelessly]. I forgot, miss. Maybe, miss, we could sort of pretend there
was pipes and pretend there was a burst, just for a lark in a manner of speakin’.
[He looks at her wistfully.]  [20]
JANE [laughing]. Don’t be antediluvian, Muggs. You must be reasonable. We live in
marvellous times, Muggs.
MUGGS [interrupting]. I agree, miss, but the more I marvels the more I yawns.
JANE [horrified]. You’re not bored, are you?
MUGGS. Yep, miss, to be frank I am.  [25]
JANE [as she busies herself with the card index]. But this is monstrous. Let me see
now. What is your number?
MUGGS. Never mind me number. Call me Muggs, Monkey Muggs, as me pals call
me.
JANE [reading from the card]. Here we are. Why, your program for the next six  [30]
months is most varied and delightful. You are to have a two month geology course
in the Isle of Skye. Then you are going on a yachting cruise to explore the migrations
of herrings and haddocks. [Muggs groans.] A course of physical exercises at
Harrogate, with evening lectures to be followed by an examination of Aristotle’s
Poetics, and finally a lovely vacation on Scottish golf courses. Muggs, how dare you  [35]
be bored!
MUGGS. Ow, miss, wot ’ave I done to deserve that?

questions.stem:
The diagram below shows an Aboriginal family tree. For the purposes of this test, the relationships between family members have been labelled according to non-Aboriginal usage. The passage explains how these same relationships are defined in Aboriginal society.

PASSAGE

In Aboriginal society the basic family unit — a man, his wife or wives, and their children — has always been very important. Basically, kinship rules considered some of the relatives of the same generation as equal, so that to an Aboriginal child the father’s brothers were all regarded as fathers, not uncles, while their male children were regarded as brothers, not cousins. On the mother’s side, her sisters were regarded as mothers, and their daughters as sisters. On the other hand, father’s sisters and mother’s brothers were regarded as aunts and uncles. An Aboriginal person thus grouped a number of relatives under a similar name. Kinship groups were recognised within each tribe, and each ‘skin group’, as it was sometimes known, had its own name and customs.

questions.stem:
The following passage is about soil erosion.

PASSAGE

Erosion by water can create deep gullies, or it can cause the soil surface of an entire mountain to slide downhill. Gullies will form along tracks that are regularly used by animals, or on ploughed land when the furrows run up and down the slope.

Erosion is mainly caused by the removal of plant cover from the soil. This may be due to overgrazing. It may also be due to forest clearance for timber or farmland.

The best way of preventing erosion is to retain or restore plant life. Plants protect the soil in many ways. Plant roots literally hold soil together and their leaf cover prevents rain from hitting the ground directly and pounding it to pieces. Farmers can help prevent erosion of newly ploughed ground by ploughing across a slope instead of up and down. In this way any soil washed down from higher ground is caught by furrows further down the slope. Clear-felling large areas of forest should be stopped and, at the same time, we should be looking for ways to reduce the number of trees we remove from forests each year.

The following poem is called Bullock Teams, by W.N. Scott. The numbers in square brackets show the line numbers.

Bullock Teams

When I was a sapling boy
bullocks still pulled the timber jinkers.
Standing, they loomed solid as mountain chains;
when they moved they leaned into the yokes,
huge wheels turned slow, hubs screamed on axles,  [5]
the great logs followed them.

But at O’Mara’s Hill, drivers tapped out their pipes,
took both hands to the whip.
The team dropped heads, backs levelled,
power poured from thrusting haunches —  [10]
they laid into it, Spot, Bally and Roger,
Blucher, Captain and patient Bob,
so tug chains rang like bells.
The logs tilted their ends to heaven
and slow as funerals, helpless as corpses,  [15]
followed the teams toward the screaming saws.

On the crest the drivers paused to blow their cattle,
to fill and light their pipes and boil the billy.
Times were hard on bullocks and men in the timber.

It’s all changed now, I have found.  [20]
You can pat and talk to a tractor all day
but it won’t look round.

W.N. Scott

questions.stem:
The following passage from a newspaper talks about a draft plan for India’s population policy.

PASSAGE

Improving schools, health services and housing, together with ‘vigorous steps’ to stamp out sexual discrimination, are the keystones of India’s draft population policy, which has just been sent to the government. The plan puts the task of improving education, health, housing and sanitation services in the lap of local councils. This will help to ‘sensitise local communities to find a balance between population and the carrying capacity of the available land’. The plan says India’s existing family planning policy fails to focus on women. It also calls for different programs for different Indian states. In Kerala, for example, women have an average of 1.8 children, compared to 5.1 in Uttar Pradesh. The plan wants the national average reduced to 2.1 by the year 2010. It calls for stricter policing of the child marriage restraint law, which bans women under 18 from marrying, and for contraception to be available to all women.
